name: Yidgha
confidence_why: Morgenstierne 1938, the only first-hand description of Yidgha, reports weak word stress overridden by sentence stress and shows the same word stressed on different syllables in different phrases, and Grjunberg 2000 agrees that Yidgha stress placement diverges from Munji's initial stress and remains unsettled, so the variable coding rests on a single thin but uncontradicted source.

catalog_quote: Stress. 39. Word stress is weak, and to some extent dominated by sentence stress. Thus, e.g.: Y sh 'wulo 'wife', but 'yū wu'lŏ 'one wife'; pisto wo zinī'ef 'she asked the daughters-in-law', but zi'nīef pi'stō 'the daughters in-law asked'; muz'durə kën 'serve'; but 'muzdu,rε γū'rum 'I take service'. Although they describe very closely related variants of M, Gauthiot and Zarubin differ considerably from each other as to the place of the accent—the Frenchman inclining to accentuate the last syllable—. My own notations, rightly or wrongly, often disagree with those of both of my predecessors, and are not always consistent. Cf. §§ 162 sqq. audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim on the page images we hold at the stated locator (pp. 34-35 sec. 39; p. 103 sec. 162). (2) The classification rests on Morgenstierne 1938, a fieldwork-based descriptive-plus-historical grammar that Glottolog itself ranks as the most extensive description of Yidgha; the only later works are a 6-page handbook sketch (Skjærvø 1989, derivative), an unpublished local sketch (1988), sociolinguistic survey material (Decker 1992), FLI text documentation (2016) and historical-comparative work (Novák 2013). (3) The one post-1938 survey chapter that covers Yidgha, Grjunberg 2000 in Jazyki mira (downloaded and scanned now, p. 170 verified on the page image), says outright that Yidgha stress 'requires further investigation' and that its place often differs from Munji, which is exactly the picture coded (no positional rule, weak word stress subordinate to sentence stress

sources.quote: p.170, verified on page image: 'Вопрос об ударении в йидга требует дополнительного исследования; во многих примерах место ударения отличается от места ударения в собственно мунджанских словах.' (The question of stress in Yidgha requires further study; in many examples the place of stress differs from that in Munji-proper words.) p.169: 'Диалект йидга изучен в синхронном плане весьма слабо.' For Munji proper, p.157 sec. 2.1.2: dynamic stress, first syllable in most native nouns, some on the second; finite verbs stressed on the stem (2nd syllable if disyllabic); inflectional markers unstressed;
sources.note: Only post-1938 survey treatment covering Yidgha; downloaded and read: confirms that Yidgha stress is undescribed beyond Morgenstierne and differs in place from Munji. Worth adding to the record as a secondary citation.

sources.quote: 'Stress is usually on the first syllable of nouns, but there are a number of exceptions where the stress placement is part of the underlying form of word and is not predictable. Words are stressed on their stems and not on their suffixes. However, the negative verbal prefix ... is always stressed. Otherwise, two-syllable verb stems are stressed on the second syllable.' sources.note: Modern first-hand stress statement for the sister lect Munji (initial default in nouns with lexical exceptions; stem stress in verbs); downloaded; useful cross-reference if Munji (munj1244) is ever ingested, silent on Yidgha.
